**Blind Vietnam Veteran Keeps Watch at Hunter Army Airfield, Welcoming Troops Home**

**By Staff Writer**  
**HUNTER ARMY AIRFIELD, Ga.** — Long before the buses pull up and the first soldiers step onto the pavement, Walt Peters is already there.

He stands near the welcome area at Hunter Army Airfield, listening for the sounds he can no longer see: the low rumble of an engine, the shuffle of boots, the sudden swell of families calling out names. When the doors open and troops return home from deployment, Peters is waiting with a handshake, a word of thanks and a smile.

When soldiers are leaving, he comes for that, too.

“Godspeed,” he tells them.

Peters, a retired Vietnam veteran, has made it his mission to be present for service members passing through Hunter Army Airfield — those coming home to loved ones and those heading out into uncertainty. Though he lost his sight after developing diabetes connected to exposure to Agent Orange during his service in Vietnam, Peters has not stepped away from the military community.

Instead, he found a new way to serve.

For years, Peters has volunteered at Hunter, offering the kind of welcome he says many Vietnam veterans never received when they returned from war. His blindness has changed how he experiences those moments, but it has not diminished their meaning.

He knows troops are approaching by the cadence of their steps. He recognizes the emotion in a spouse’s voice before an embrace. He hears children break into laughter when a parent appears. And he understands the quiet weight carried by soldiers who are leaving, even when few words are spoken.

To Peters, showing up matters.

He served in Vietnam at a time when many returning veterans were met not with gratitude, but with anger, indifference or silence. That memory remains part of what drives him to greet today’s troops. If a soldier returns home through Hunter Army Airfield, Peters wants that soldier to know someone was waiting.

The work is simple but deeply personal. He shakes hands. He thanks them for their service. He offers encouragement to young soldiers deploying for the first time and reassurance to families watching them go. He stands with other volunteers, military supporters and loved ones during ceremonies that are often brief but emotional.

For deploying troops, Peters’ message is steady: do your duty, take care of one another and come home safe.

For returning troops, it is even simpler: welcome home.

Those two words carry special weight coming from a Vietnam veteran. Peters understands how much they can mean because he remembers a time when they were rarely said.

His service also came with a lasting cost. Like many Vietnam veterans, Peters was exposed to Agent Orange, the herbicide used by the U.S. military during the war and later linked by the Department of Veterans Affairs to several serious health conditions, including Type 2 diabetes. Peters’ diabetes eventually contributed to the loss of his sight.

But he does not frame his blindness as the end of his usefulness.

At Hunter Army Airfield, he remains a familiar presence — a veteran continuing to serve in the company of newer generations. He cannot see the soldiers’ uniforms, the flags, the hugs or the tears, but he can feel the purpose of the moment.

And those who see him there often understand something before he says a word: Peters has earned the right to stay home, to rest and to let others do the welcoming.

He comes anyway.

For families waiting through the final minutes before reunion, Peters is part of the scene — a reminder that military service stretches across generations. For young soldiers, he represents a living connection to a war many know only from history books. For fellow veterans, he is proof that service does not always end with discharge or retirement.

At every homecoming, Peters listens as families surge forward. At every departure, he offers the same quiet blessing.

“Godspeed,” he says again.

And then he waits for the next group of troops — some leaving, some returning — making sure none of them pass through unnoticed.

**At an Army airfield, a 64-year-old veteran has greeted thousands of troops — one small flag at a time**

By the time the buses pull up to the Army airfield, the soldiers are usually tired.

Some are headed overseas, carrying rucksacks packed with gear and the weight of what comes next. Others are coming home, stepping off aircraft into the first familiar air they’ve breathed in months. Many are quiet. Some are smiling. A few look stunned to be back.

Waiting for them is a 64-year-old veteran with a box of small American flags.

He doesn’t give speeches. He doesn’t ask for attention. He simply stands there — often before sunrise, sometimes late at night — offering a handshake, a few words of thanks and a flag small enough to fit in a uniform pocket.

Over the years, he estimates he has greeted about 20,000 soldiers at the airfield.

“I just want them to know somebody is here,” he said. “Whether they’re leaving or coming home, they deserve to be seen.”

For many of the troops moving through the installation, the moment is brief: a flag, a nod, a “welcome home” or “stay safe.” But for the veteran and the network of volunteers he helps organize, it is part of a larger mission — one built around showing service members that their sacrifice is recognized long before the parades, ceremonies and holidays.

The effort has grown from a handful of people showing up when they could into a coordinated volunteer operation. He helps arrange greeters for troop movements, connects families with support programs and works with an Adopt-A-Soldier initiative that sends care packages, letters and everyday supplies to deployed service members.

The items are simple — snacks, toiletries, socks, notes from schoolchildren — but volunteers say the message behind them is what matters most.

“It tells a soldier, ‘You have not been forgotten,’” the veteran said.

On busy days, volunteers line the airfield area holding flags and signs. Some are veterans themselves. Others are military spouses, retirees, students or community members who have no direct tie to the armed forces but want to help.

They learn to be flexible. Flights change. Buses run late. Weather turns. Sometimes soldiers arrive when most of the surrounding community is asleep. The veteran is often the one making calls, checking schedules and making sure someone is there.

He knows what it feels like to serve and come home to uncertainty. That experience, he said, is part of what drives him.

“You remember the faces,” he said. “You remember who was there for you — and who wasn’t. So if I can be there for somebody else, I’m going to be there.”

The flags have become his signature.

He buys them in bulk when he can, accepts donations when people offer and keeps them ready for the next arrival or departure. Each one is handed out the same way: personally, respectfully, with a thank-you.

Some soldiers tuck them into helmets or backpacks. Some hand them to their children. Others hold them silently as they step toward waiting family members.

There are moments that stay with him: a young soldier gripping the flag before boarding a plane; a parent breaking down at the sight of a returning son; a service member who came back months later and remembered him.

“They’ll say, ‘You were here when we left,’” he said. “That means something.”

The Adopt-A-Soldier program has widened that reach beyond the airfield. Through the effort, volunteers “adopt” deployed troops or units, sending packages and letters throughout deployments. The veteran helps coordinate donors, gather supplies and match support with soldiers who may need it most.

Community groups often pitch in. Churches collect hygiene items. Schools write cards. Local businesses donate shipping money or supplies. Families help pack boxes. The veteran sees it as a bridge between the military and the civilians who want to support it but may not know how.

“Not everybody can stand at the airfield,” he said. “But everybody can do something.”

For the volunteers, his commitment sets the pace.

They describe him as steady — the person who answers the phone, sends the reminder, shows up early and stays until the last soldier has passed through. He is quick to credit others, insisting the work belongs to the community. But those around him say his example is what keeps the effort moving.

“He makes sure no one walks through alone,” one volunteer said.

At 64, he has no plans to stop.

There will be more early mornings, more delayed flights, more boxes to pack and more flags to hand out. There will be more soldiers leaving for places their families can only imagine, and more returning home changed by what they’ve seen.

And if he can help it, someone will be waiting.

“I can’t change what they’re going into,” he said. “I can’t take away what they’ve been through. But I can stand there, look them in the eye and say, ‘Thank you.’ Sometimes that’s the least we can do. Sometimes it’s exactly what they need.”

## On the Homefront in Savannah: Walt Peters’ Long Watch for America’s Troops

**SAVANNAH, Ga. —** Before sunrise, when the streets near Savannah’s historic squares are still quiet and the air carries the damp salt of the Georgia coast, Walt Peters is already where he believes he belongs: close to the soldiers.

He cannot see the buses when they roll in. He cannot see the uniforms, the duffel bags, the anxious faces of young men and women preparing to leave for war, or the tearful families waiting for them to return. But Peters knows the sounds. The low rumble of engines. The clipped movement of boots. The murmured prayers. The laughter that tries to cover fear. The silence that follows a last embrace.

For years, Peters has made it his mission to support U.S. service members passing through Savannah on their way to and from deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. Blindness may have taken his sight, but it did not dim his sense of duty. A Vietnam veteran, Peters understands better than most what it means to go to war — and what it means to come home.

His presence on the homefront has become a quiet symbol of continuity between generations of American service members: those who fought in Vietnam, those who deployed after September 11, and the families who waited for them all.

### A Vietnam Veteran Who Never Stopped Serving

Walt Peters’ military story began decades before the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Like many young Americans of his generation, he served during the Vietnam era, a conflict that left deep marks on the men who fought it and on the nation that sent them.

Vietnam veterans often returned to a country divided over the war. Many came home without parades, without public thanks, and sometimes without the understanding or support they needed. For Peters, that experience became part of the reason he later dedicated himself to a different kind of mission.

He knew the weight of a deployment. He knew the fear a soldier can carry but not speak aloud. He knew how much it matters to be met not with politics, but with gratitude.

His own life was also shaped by blindness, a challenge that might have led others to retreat from public service. Peters did the opposite. Instead of allowing blindness to narrow his world, he expanded his commitment. He found ways to be present, to encourage, to listen, and to remind deploying troops that someone at home cared enough to show up.

In the process, he became part of Savannah’s military support network — one of those civilians and veterans whose names may not appear in official histories, but whose impact is remembered by soldiers and families.

### Savannah’s Role in America’s Wars

Savannah has long been a military city. Its proximity to major Army installations, including Fort Stewart and Hunter Army Airfield, ties the coastal Georgia community closely to the rhythms of military life. When America went to war in Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003, the region felt it immediately.
